note: Plain-English glossary. Terms are surfaced inline as tooltips and in the glossary drawer.

terms.short: The person who carries out your will.
terms.long: Your executor collects your assets, pays debts and funeral costs, then gives people what you left them. It is a real job — usually a few months of paperwork. Choose someone organised, and ask them first.

terms.short: The person who looks after money held on trust.
terms.long: Usually the same person as your executor. If anything is held for a child or a vulnerable beneficiary, the trustee manages it until the right time.

terms.short: Anyone who receives something under your will.
terms.long: A beneficiary can be a person, a charity, or a trust. Beneficiaries should never witness your will — a gift to a witness is void.

terms.short: Everything left after debts, expenses and specific gifts.
terms.long: Usually the largest part of a will — the family home, superannuation paid to the estate, savings. Your 'residue clause' decides who receives it.

terms.short: A particular item or amount you leave to someone.
terms.long: For example a ring, a car, or $5,000. Specific gifts are paid out before the residue is divided, so large gifts can reduce what's left for everyone else.

terms.short: When a gift fails because the item no longer exists.
terms.long: If you leave someone your car and sell it before you die, the gift simply fails — they get nothing in its place unless your will says otherwise.

terms.short: The person who would raise your children.
terms.long: A testamentary guardian makes day-to-day decisions for children under 18. A surviving parent with parental responsibility usually continues regardless, so a guardian normally matters only if both parents have died.

terms.short: The legal authority to make decisions for a child.
terms.long: Most parents have it automatically. Court orders can limit it. It affects how much weight your guardian nomination carries.

terms.short: The court's approval that lets your executor act.
terms.long: A grant of probate from the Supreme Court of Queensland confirms your will is valid and your executor may deal with banks, property and investments.

terms.short: What happens when someone dies without a valid will.
terms.long: A legislated formula decides who inherits — not you. It often surprises families, and rarely matches what people would have chosen.

terms.short: A trust created by your will.
terms.long: Instead of handing money over outright, it's held and managed for a beneficiary — useful for young people, vulnerable beneficiaries, or tax planning.

terms.short: A trust that protects a vulnerable beneficiary.
terms.long: If a beneficiary receives a pension, NDIS support or has difficulty managing money, a direct inheritance can do harm. A protective trust holds it for their benefit instead.

terms.short: A court application for a bigger share of an estate.
terms.long: In Queensland a spouse, child or dependant left out of a will — or left very little — can apply to the court for provision. Recording your reasons carefully is the best protection.

terms.short: Co-ownership where the survivor automatically takes all.
terms.long: If you own your home as joint tenants, your share passes straight to the other owner when you die — your will does not control it.

terms.short: Co-ownership where your share passes under your will.
terms.long: Each owner has a distinct share. Your share forms part of your estate and goes to whoever your will says.

terms.short: A form telling your super fund who gets your super.
terms.long: Superannuation is not automatically part of your estate. A valid binding nomination overrides your will for that money, so the two need to line up.

terms.short: A backup instruction if a gift fails.
terms.long: For example: 'to my sister, but if she dies before me, to her children'. Gift-over clauses stop a share falling into intestacy.

terms.short: A formal amendment to an existing will.
terms.long: A codicil must be signed and witnessed with the same ceremony as a will. These days it is usually cleaner to make a fresh will.

terms.short: Cancelling an earlier will.
terms.long: Most wills begin by revoking all earlier wills. In Queensland, marriage generally revokes a will too, unless it was made in contemplation of that marriage.

terms.short: The signing and witnessing section of a will.
terms.long: The attestation clause records that you signed in front of two adult witnesses who were both present at the same time — the formality that makes a will valid.

terms.short: Someone who watches you sign your will.
terms.long: You need two, both 18 or over, both present at the same time. Neither may be a beneficiary or the spouse of a beneficiary, or their gift is void.

terms.short: Being of sound mind when you make your will.
terms.long: You must understand that you are making a will, roughly what you own, and who might expect to benefit. Your lawyer considers this for every client.

terms.short: Being pressured into making a will you didn't want.
terms.long: If someone pressures a will-maker, the will can be set aside. It's why we ask whether anyone is helping you, and whether they benefit.

terms.short: Everything you own at the moment you die.
terms.long: Your estate includes property, savings, investments and possessions — but usually not superannuation, life insurance paid to a person, or jointly-owned property.
